terms.p: The single binding responsible for a value. When it goes out of scope the value is dropped, which is how Rust knows when to free memory without a garbage collector.
Transferring ownership from one binding to another. It copies the small fixed-size handle, not the heap contents, and the old binding becomes unusable.
Transferring ownership from one binding to another. It copies the small fixed-size handle, not the heap contents, and the old binding becomes unusable.

terms.x: the stack part of a heap value
terms.p: The small fixed-size struct that lives on the stack and points at heap contents. For a String, that is the pointer, the length and the capacity.
Receiving a value itself rather than a reference to it, which transfers ownership to the receiver.
A marker meaning a value can be duplicated by copying its bytes, so assignment leaves the original usable. Only for types that own nothing needing cleanup.
An explicit duplicate via .clone(), which may allocate. Unlike Copy it never happens implicitly, so the cost is always visible in the source.
The automatic cleanup that runs when an owner goes out of scope: it releases the value's resources, freeing heap memory, closing files, unlocking mutexes.
A hidden boolean the compiler inserts when it cannot tell statically whether a value was moved, so it knows at runtime whether to drop it. Usually optimised away.
Bindings in a scope are dropped last-declared-first, because later values are the ones most likely to depend on earlier ones.
Returning the same allocation to the allocator twice. It corrupts the allocator's bookkeeping and is a reliable route from a memory bug to an exploit.
Reading memory that has already been handed back to the allocator, which may since have been given to something else entirely.
Tying a resource to a value's lifetime, so acquiring the value acquires the resource and dropping it releases the resource. Cleanup happens on every exit path without being written at any of them.
Taking a reference to a value: permission to use it without owning it. The value cannot be moved or dropped while the borrow is live.
A pointer the compiler guarantees is valid and non-null for as long as you can use it. Shared (&T) or unique (&mut T), never both at once.
A read-only borrow. Many may exist at once, and none of them may mutate what they point at.
A unique borrow that permits mutation. Exactly one may exist at a time, and no shared reference may coexist with it.
A named region of code over which a reference is guaranteed valid. It describes a claim the compiler checks, not a duration you set.
The rules that let you omit lifetime annotations in common function signatures, because the compiler can infer the only sensible answer.
A reference to memory that no longer holds the value it was made from. Rust rejects these at compile time rather than crashing on them.
A borrowed view of a contiguous run of elements: a pointer plus a length, pointing into something someone else owns.
A pointer carrying a second word of metadata: a length for slices, a vtable address for trait objects.
A growable, heap-allocated, UTF-8 string that owns its buffer. The owned counterpart to &str.
A borrowed view of UTF-8 bytes. It can point into a String, into a literal in the binary, or into part of either.
A growable heap-allocated array that owns its elements: pointer, length and capacity, exactly like String.
How many elements a Vec or String has room for before it must reallocate. Always at least its length, and usually more.
Per-call memory, pushed on entry and popped on return. Fast, and only usable for values whose size is known at compile time.
Memory requested at runtime for values whose size or lifetime the stack cannot accommodate. Someone must decide when to give it back; in Rust the owner does.
A named set of methods a type can implement. Rust's answer to interfaces, and the basis of both generics and dynamic dispatch.
A value behind a pointer whose concrete type is not known at compile time, carrying a vtable so calls can be dispatched at runtime.
The compiler emitting one specialised copy of a generic function per concrete type used, which is why generic Rust costs nothing at runtime.
Resolving which function to call at compile time, so the call can be inlined. What generics give you.
Looking up which function to call through a vtable at runtime. What trait objects give you, at the cost of an indirection.
Implementing a trait for every type satisfying some bound at once, such as impl<T: Display> ToString for T.
The restriction that a trait impl must be in the crate defining either the trait or the type, so two crates cannot supply conflicting impls.
Code written against a type parameter rather than a concrete type, specialised by the compiler for each type actually used.
A constraint saying a type parameter must implement a given trait, which is what makes the parameter's methods callable.
A value that is either Some(T) or None. Rust's replacement for null, and the compiler makes you handle the empty case.
A value that is either Ok(T) or Err(E). Errors are ordinary return values, so ignoring one is visible in the source.
An unrecoverable failure that unwinds the stack, running destructors as it goes. For bugs, not for expected error conditions.
Shorthand that returns early with the error if a Result is Err, and otherwise unwraps the Ok value.
The requirement that a match covers every possible case, which turns adding an enum variant into a compile error at every place that must change.
A type that is exactly one of several named variants, each able to carry its own data. Far more useful than a C enum.
Destructuring a value by its shape and binding its parts, checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler.
Declaring a new binding with the same name as an existing one. The old value still exists; the name simply refers to the new one.
Mutating through a shared reference, with the borrow rule moved from compile time to runtime and enforced by a panic instead of an error.
The simplest owning pointer: it puts a value on the heap and frees it when dropped. Used for recursive types and for trait objects.
A reference-counted shared owner for single-threaded code. The value is dropped when the last Rc goes away.
Rc with an atomic counter, so it can be shared across threads. Slightly slower, and the only one that is Send.
A container that enforces the borrow rules at runtime instead of compile time, panicking if you break them.
A marker meaning a value is safe to move to another thread. Almost everything is; Rc is the notable exception.
A marker meaning a value is safe to reference from several threads at once, which is the same thing as saying that &T is Send.
Two threads touching the same memory at the same time with at least one writing. Rust's borrow rules make this a compile error.
An anonymous function that captures variables from its surrounding scope, by reference or by value depending on what it does with them.
A value producing items one at a time via next(). Lazy by construction: adapters build a description, and nothing runs until something consumes it.
An abstraction that compiles to the same machine code you would have written by hand, so using it costs nothing at runtime.
A block where five extra operations are permitted, such as dereferencing a raw pointer. It does not disable the borrow checker; it moves responsibility for the invariants to you.
A state the language makes no promises about, where the compiler may assume it cannot happen and optimise accordingly. The thing safe Rust exists to prevent.
The unit the compiler builds at once: either a library or a binary. A package may contain several.
A named namespace inside a crate, controlling which items are visible outside it.
A named opt-in set of language changes, such as 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2024. Crates on different editions interoperate freely.
Rust's build system and package manager: it resolves dependencies, compiles, tests, benchmarks and publishes.
The compiler pass that verifies every reference is valid for as long as it is used and that no two conflicting borrows overlap.
To emit a specialised copy of generic code for each concrete type it is used with.
A value representing work that is not finished. It does nothing until polled, which is why an async function that is never awaited never runs.
Syntax that turns a function into a state machine returning a Future, so the thread can do something else while it waits.
Code that writes code, expanded before type checking. Declarative macros match on syntax; procedural macros run arbitrary Rust at compile time.
The ::<Type> syntax for supplying type arguments explicitly where inference cannot decide, as in parse::<i32>().
A single-field tuple struct wrapping another type, used to add meaning or to implement a foreign trait without breaking coherence.
A table of function pointers carried alongside a trait object so the right implementation can be found at runtime.
